title: How HTTPS Keeps Your Data Private

narration: Imagine you press Submit on a login form.
A watcher sits somewhere on the path.
What does it see?
beats.visual_intent: One light board: a browser card on the left with a form and a Submit button, a server card on the right, a slate router box between them with a watcher marker. On Submit, a packet carrying readable text leaves the browser along the path.

grounding.claim: A form submission crosses devices on the path with a watcher among them (illustrative)

narration: Plain web traffic is readable text.
Any device on the path can copy it.
beats.visual_intent: The packet passes the watcher box, which duplicates it; the copy shows the same readable form fields, held beside the original so both read identically.

grounding.claim: Plain HTTP traffic is readable text
Devices on the path can copy what passes; nothing prevents it

narration: Follow one request, and learn what the padlock means.
beats.visual_intent: The same board holds still; a small open padlock icon appears above the path and the watcher's copy blurs slightly as a promise of the outcome, without changing the layout.

grounding.claim: Promise of the lesson's outcome (padlock meaning)

narration: First, the browser asks the server who it is.
It sends a certificate naming its site.
A certificate authority vouches for it.
beats.visual_intent: A request arrow runs from browser to server; a certificate card slides back to the browser showing a site name and a small authority seal that appears on the last phrase.

grounding.claim: Browser asks server to identify itself, server answers with a certificate
Certificate states the site name and is vouched for by a trusted authority

narration: The browser checks three things.
The name matches. It has not expired.
The issuer is trusted.
beats.visual_intent: On the certificate card at the browser, three teal ticks appear one at a time beside name, expiry and issuer fields, each on its phrase.

grounding.claim: Browser checks name match, expiry and trusted issuer

narration: Next, both sides agree a shared key.
It is never sent in the open.
beats.visual_intent: The certificate card shrinks to a ticked badge; an empty key slot appears at each end of the path, with the watcher still between them.

grounding.claim: Browser and server agree a shared key; the key itself is never sent in the open

narration: Each side sends a value across.
The watcher copies both, but cannot find the key.
beats.visual_intent: Two small value tokens cross the path in opposite directions; the watcher copies each into a tray, and a blank key slot stays empty beside the watcher.

grounding.claim: Values sent in the open are not enough for a watcher to work out the key

narration: Both ends now hold the same key.
The watcher does not.
beats.visual_intent: Matching blue keys appear in the slots at browser and server only; the watcher's slot remains empty.

grounding.claim: Both ends hold the same key, the watcher does not

narration: The key counts only after all three checks pass.
beats.visual_intent: The ticked badge enlarges beside the keys and its three ticks re-light in turn, tying the key to the passed check.

recall.answer: Name matches, not expired, trusted issuer.

grounding.claim: Three certificate checks recalled

narration: HTTPS is web traffic inside an encrypted connection.
Encryption scrambles the form with the key.
beats.visual_intent: The form data block at the browser, readable, passes through the blue key and turns into scrambled blocks as it leaves.

grounding.claim: HTTPS is HTTP inside an encrypted TLS connection
Encryption turns readable data into scrambled data using a key
Browser encrypts the form submission with the key

narration: Scrambled blocks pass the watcher unchanged.
It sees noise, and usually which server.
beats.visual_intent: Scrambled blocks travel past the watcher, whose copy is the same unreadable pattern; a small label shows the server address still visible, content not.

grounding.claim: Watcher sees only scrambled data; usually still sees which server

narration: The server decrypts it with the same key.
Replies are protected both ways.
beats.visual_intent: At the server the scrambled blocks pass the key and turn readable again; a reply packet then travels back as scrambled blocks and turns readable at the browser.

grounding.claim: Server decrypts with the same key
Replies are protected the same way in both directions

narration: A site's certificate names a different site.
Continue quietly, warn you, or switch to plain?
beats.visual_intent: The same request goes to a new server whose certificate card shows a different name; three option cards appear side by side on their phrases, none marked.

recall.prompt: A site's certificate was issued for a different name than the address bar. What should the browser do?
options: Warn you and not continue silently

grounding.claim: Failed name check scenario

narration: It warns you, and does not continue silently.
Overriding the warning removes the identity check.
beats.visual_intent: The name tick on the certificate card turns red and the warning option card lights; the continue-quietly card dims with a note that scrambling alone leaves the far end unknown.

grounding.claim: On a failed check the browser warns and does not continue silently by default
Overriding removes the identity check

narration: The padlock means the link is encrypted,
and the certificate matched that site name.
beats.visual_intent: An address bar appears with a generic padlock; two teal labels attach to the padlock on the two phrases.

grounding.claim: Padlock indicates an encrypted connection and an accepted certificate for that site name

narration: It does not show the owner is honest.
Nor does it protect data after it arrives.
beats.visual_intent: Two slate 'does not show' labels are added beside the padlock; the server card at the end of the path shows the form data readable again.

grounding.claim: Padlock does not show the owner is honest or trustworthy
No protection once data has arrived

narration: Before typing, read the site name exactly.
Check that no certificate warning shows.
Look-alike names are a common trick.
beats.visual_intent: Two ticks are added in the address bar: the site name is highlighted letter by letter, then a warning banner slot is shown empty.

grounding.claim: Check the exact site name and absence of a certificate warning; look-alike names are a common trick

narration: Back to the form: same data, same watcher.
Now it copies only scrambled noise,
and the padlock closes.
beats.visual_intent: The opening board returns unchanged: form, path, watcher. The packet crosses as scrambled blocks, the watcher's copy is noise, and the padlock above the path closes.

grounding.claim: Watcher sees only scrambled data
Padlock indicates an encrypted connection
